Biography
I’m originally from a small town in Newfoundland, called Harbour Grace. Growing up I loved math and science, so when I had the chance I decided to pursue those subjects in university. For my BSc (Joint Hons) in Applied Math and Physics, I completed research in numerical methods for adaptive mesh generation. This research was conducted under the supervision of Dr. Ronald Haynes. Next, I completed my MSc in Math under the supervision of Dr. Hari Kunduri. This research focused on theoretical black holes and their geometry. My BEd in Intermediate/Secondary Education was completed as I finished my MSc. This included a teaching internship at Prince of Wales Collegiate in St. John’s, NL.
Since then, I’ve taught post‑secondary mathematics at the College of the North Atlantic, worked as a Health Information Specialist at Health PEI (statistical analysis and data visualization), and joined Holland College as a Learning Manager of Mathematics and Physics. I serve as a Faculty Representative on the college’s Accessability and Inclusion Advisory Council, The City of Charlottetown’s Affordable Housing Advisory Board, and as a trustee of the Public Schools Branch (PEI), where I chair the Finance & Audit Committee.



In my spare time I enjoy spending time outside. This includes relaxing beach trips or day long hiking expeditions. Growing up in Newfoundland gives one ample opportunity to explore nature and I’m lucky to continue doing so on beautiful Prince Edward Island. I live in Charlottetown with my wife and our six pets (2 dogs and 4 cats).

articles.title: Academic Publications
articles.contents:
Theses
MSc (Mathematics)
Title: Constructing Static Black Hole–Soliton Spacetimes
Supervisor: Dr. Hari Kunduri
Institution: Memorial University of Newfoundland
Year: 2019
Abstract: This thesis explores the construction of static black hole–soliton spacetimes in general relativity. We investigate solutions to Einstein’s field equations that combine both black hole and soliton components, examining their geometric properties and physical significance in higher-dimensional theories of gravity.
